questions.question: Describe the life and work of enslaved people at the Cape.
questions.expected_answer: Worked on wine and wheat farms (ploughing, harvesting, pruning vines, making wine, herding, building) or in Cape Town households and trades (domestic servants, washerwomen, porters, fishermen, carpenters, masons, coopers); women did field work and housework and cared for owners' children; long hours, basic food, poor housing, no shoes; passes and lanterns at night; could not legally marry or own property; families could be sold apart; harsh punishment including whipping and brutal public punishment for rebellion; yet formed families and communities, and some gained manumission.

questions.question: Explain how Islam was established at the Cape.
questions.expected_answer: Brought by enslaved people from Indonesia and India and by political exiles and convicts; Sheikh Yusuf of Makassar exiled 1694 to Zandvliet (Macassar), regarded as founder of Islam in SA; Tuan Guru, imprisoned on Robben Island 1780-1793, wrote the Qur'an from memory, founded the first madrasah (1793) and the Auwal Mosque in Bo-Kaap (1794); practised privately as public worship was forbidden by the VOC; spread because it offered community, dignity, education and literacy.

questions.question: Explain the contribution of enslaved people to Afrikaans and Cape culture.
questions.expected_answer: Afrikaans developed from Dutch as spoken by enslaved people from Africa and Asia, Khoikhoi and settlers, taking words from Malay (baie, piering, pisang), Portuguese creole and Khoekhoegowab, and simplified grammar - a creole language; early written Afrikaans was produced by Cape Muslims in Arabic script (Arabic-Afrikaans). Other legacies: Cape cuisine (bobotie, bredie, sosaties, koeksisters), Cape Dutch architecture by skilled craftsmen, music such as the Kaapse Klopse, and surnames.
